etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English stageren, stakeren, from Old Norse stakra (“to push, stagger”). Cognate with dialectal Danish stagre.

definitions.definition: An unsteady movement of the body in walking or standing as if one were about to fall; a reeling motion.

quote.citation: 7 October 2012, Paolo Bandini in The Guardian, Denver Broncos 21 New England Patriots 31 - as it happened
quote.text: Put down the rosary beads folks, I believe hell may just have frozen over. Peyton Manning drops back, sees nothing open and runs for a first down. If you can call that running. More like the stagger of a wounded rhino. Did the job, though

quote.citation: 1861, Ellen Wood, chapter 39, in East Lynne:
quote.text: Afy slowly gathered in the sense of the words. She gasped twice, as if her breath had gone, and then, with a stagger and a shiver, fell heavily to the ground.

quote.citation: 1843 December 19, Charles Dickens, “(please specify the page number)”, in A Christmas Carol. In Prose. Being a Ghost Story of Christmas, London: Chapman & Hall, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: And when old Fezziwig and Mrs. Fezziwig had gone all through the dance; advance and retire; both hands to your partner, bow and courtesy, corkscrew, thread the needle, and back again to your place; Fezziwig "cut"—cut so deftly that he appeared to wink with his legs, and came upon his feet again without a stagger.

definitions.definition: (veterinary medicine) A disease of horses and other animals, attended by reeling, unsteady gait or sudden falling.
The spacing out of various actions over time.

quote.citation: 19 April 2016, Rachel Roddy in The Guardian, Rachel Roddy’s Roman spring vegetable stew recipe
quote.text: I don’t include cured pork, although it is very nice, and rather than putting everything in the pan at once I prefer a stagger of ingredients, which ensures each one gets the right amount of time.

definitions.definition: (motor racing) The difference in circumference between the left and right tires on a racing vehicle. It is used on oval tracks to make the car turn better in the corners.[2]
(aviation) The horizontal positioning of a biplane, triplane, or multiplane's wings in relation to one another.
(intransitive) In standing or walking, to sway from one side to the other as if about to fall; to stand or walk unsteadily; to reel or totter.

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “Palamon and Arcite”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Deep was the wound; he staggered with the blow.

quote.citation: 2022 January 12, Benedict le Vay, “The heroes of Soham...”, in RAIL, number 948, page 43:
quote.text: The burnt and bleeding man staggered to his feet, dazed and unbelieving, and asked the startled townspeople who came running whether his fireman and guard were safe. He was kept away from the smouldering crater where his engine had been, and taken to hospital.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cause to reel or totter.

quote.citation: 1595 December 9 (first known performance), William Shakespeare, “The life and death of King Richard the Second”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies: Published According to the True Originall Copies (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene v]:
quote.text: That hand shall burn in never-quenching fire / That staggers thus my person.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To cease to stand firm; to begin to give way; to fail.
To sway unsteadily, reel, or totter.
(intransitive) To begin to doubt and waver in purposes; to become less confident or determined; to hesitate.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Romans 4:20:
quote.text: He [Abraham] staggered not at the promise of God through unbelief.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cause to doubt and waver; to make to hesitate; to make less steady or confident; to shock.

quote.citation: 1644, James Howell, England’s Teares, for the Present Wars, […], London:  […]  Richard Heron, →OCLC, page 6:
quote.text: [W]hoſoever vvill be curious to read the future ſtory of this intricate VVarre (if it be poſsible to compile a ſtory of it) he vvill find himſelfe much ſtagger'd, and put to a kind of riddle;  […]

quote.citation: 1796, Edmund Burke, A Letter from the Right Honourable Edmund Burke to a Noble Lord, on the Attacks Made upon Him and His Pension, […], 10th edition, London:  […]  J. Owen, […], and F[rancis] and C[harles] Rivington, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Grants to the house of Russell were so enormous, as not only to outrage economy, but even to stagger credibility.

quote.citation: 1943 September and October, “Post-War London Terminals”, in Railway Magazine, page 257:
quote.text: Unless it is intended to divert much of the Southern suburban traffic underground, the size of the structure needed to handle all the Southern Railway suburban, outer suburban, and main-line traffic in one station staggers the imagination.

definitions.definition: To arrange (a series of parts) on each side of a median line alternately, as the spokes of a wheel or the rivets of a boiler seam.
To arrange similar objects such that each is ahead or above and to one side of the next.
To schedule in intervals or at different times.

quote.citation: 1962 September, “Talking of Trains: More commuters by rail”, in Modern Railways, page 154:
quote.text: The evening peak (5.30-5.45) is more concentrated than the morning (9–9.15), but it had not been intensified in the 12 months to last November; this is attributed by London Transport partly to efforts to persuade firms to stagger their hours.

definitions.definition: (transitive) Have multiple groups doing the same thing in a uniform fashion, but starting at different, evenly spaced, times or places (attested from 1856[3]).

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From stag +‎ -er.

definitions.definition: (UK) One who attends a stag night.

quote.citation: 2013, Phil Hubbard, Cities and Sexualities, page 144:
quote.text: Tallinn no longer takes pride in the title of 'favourite destination of British staggers'.
